Maladaptive Strategies.value: rehearse what to say before any interaction
cut off all contact with friends and family

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

I can no longer trust my own body

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-themed conversations are hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 51-year-old school principal; this trigger implies a combat-related context not represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
issues.explanation: Avoiding people involved in the event or who look similar fits interpersonal/assault/accident traumas better than life-threatening illness, where there are typically no 'other people involved' in that sense. It is not well supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'talking about the future' as a trigger is plausible, but 'alcohol smell' is hard to connect unless alcohol was part of treatment context; nothing else in the profile supports that association, making this trigger set clinically incoherent.

'People can't be trusted' is more typical of interpersonal trauma and is poorly anchored to a life-threatening illness trauma in the absence of any treatment-related betrayal, conflict, or mistrust themes elsewhere in the profile.

'Crying' is not a trauma cue but an affective response/behavior, so it is clinically incoherent as a trigger item relative to the other trigger items, which are concrete sensory reminders linked to life-threatening illness (alcohol smell, hospital/antiseptic smell).

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: A global mistrust appraisal is a poor fit for the rest of the profile and trauma type. In life-threatening illness, the other items center on altered self and self-reliance, while 'People can't be trusted' implies an interpersonal betrayal/threat theme that is not supported by the memory, trigger, or strategy items and does not align well with the otherwise weak/inactive Threat links.

vignette: Thomas, a 51‑year‑old school principal in a Midwestern district, was abruptly confronted with a life‑threatening illness in the spring of 2018. He slipped in a hallway while reviewing a teacher’s report card, hit his head on a doorframe, and later collapsed in the hallway, his heart failing for a brief moment. The emergency response team pulled him into a fluorescent‑lit emergency room where the antiseptic smell of disinfectant and the sharp sting of IV drips filled his senses. While he lay on the gurney, a faint scent of alcohol from the recovery room’s lounge drifted toward him, the same scent Thomas had associated with the hospital’s post‑operative recovery bar. Those odors, the sterile hospital air, and the mechanical whirring of the infusion pump instantly triggered a flood of unease that surged into the next week. The triggers made Thomas hypervigilant: he began rehearsing what he would say whenever he had to discuss health matters with colleagues or parents, isolated himself from friends and family to avoid being in any place that might smell of antiseptic, and, when a staff member asked him to come in for a routine check‑up, he declined and later cancelled an invitation to a staff meeting. In those moments, the smell of alcohol, hospital air, or a medical procedure would surface in his mind, and the memory of the emergency room would surface without clear images, leaving him with a visceral emotional intensity that felt as if the heart was still pounding. The triggers had not only sparked the maladaptive strategies but also opened the door to the memory of the event, and Thomas felt that the hospital had turned his body into an unreliable alarm system. The negative appraisal that “the person I have become is unrecognisable to me” ran through Thomas’s thoughts whenever a familiar scent rose. He could no longer trust that his own body would signal danger correctly; he feared that the next time he inhaled the scent of antiseptic, the next time he heard the hiss of a pump, his body might betray him again. This belief hardened into a conviction that he could not rely on himself, and that the body had betrayed him once, it would betray him again. The fear of his own body’s unreliability magnified the anxiety triggered by any medical cue, pushing him further into isolation. It also made it harder for him to recall details of that hospital day: he could think of the sounds and the feelings, but could not bring a clear image into view. Thomas’s belief that he was no longer trustworthy to his own instincts spurred him to rehearse conversations about health at home, and the rehearsals turned into a ritual that reinforced the negative self‑image that he could not be his own reliable guide. When the memory of the emergency room seeped into Thomas’s mind during a quiet night, it did not arrive as a clear visual. Instead, he felt the body’s familiar posture, the way his arms were positioned, the stiffness of his spine, as though he were again in that fluorescent hallway, his heart racing beneath a white coat. The bodily reenactment made him feel as though he were back in that instant, and that experience triggered a surge of the same terror he had felt then. The emotional intensity without a clear image spurred Thomas to rehearse what he would say in front of a mirror, and he became convinced that he needed to control every word, to prove to himself that he could still be safe. The memory’s vague, visceral quality only deepened his negative appraisal that his body was unreliable, a belief that seemed to echo the physical sensations he now expected to feel with any trigger. Thomas’s rehearsed conversations grew into a rigid script that he would recite with a mechanical calm in the staff lounge or at the parent‑teacher conference. The script, though carefully crafted, made him feel like a character in a play rather than himself, reinforcing the appraisal that the person he had become was unrecognisable. The isolation, a product of his own avoidance, made him feel as though he could not rely on others for support, and the avoidance of medical cues – refusing to answer calls about his health, canceling appointments – fed into the belief that his own body would betray him again. The maladaptive strategies fed back into the negative appraisal loop, each rehearsal, each isolated dinner, each missed appointment reinforcing the notion that he could not trust himself, that his body was a false alarm. In the spring of 2021, while Thomas was preparing a lesson plan for his high school science class, a sudden burst of panic erupted when the hallway’s fluorescent lights flickered, and the faint antiseptic odor drifted in from a nearby nurse’s office. The trigger was immediate and unavoidable; it was the same scent that had haunted him since 2018. He could feel his heart pound in a rhythm he remembered from the emergency room, the memory flaring up without clear images, and his rehearsed script for how to handle such incidents began to take hold. The panic, the body’s re‑enactment, and the smell of antiseptic pushed him to cancel the class, to isolate from the staff, and to avoid any future medical cues that might surface in the school environment. The chain of events felt endless, as though the triggers, memories, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies were locked together in a tight spiral. Thomas’s decision to seek therapy was finally prompted by the night he slept in his office, staring at the ceiling and feeling as though the hospital’s antiseptic air was permeating his personal space. He realized that his avoidance of medical cues had prevented him from leading his school, from engaging with his staff, and from attending the graduation ceremony where he would speak. He is now fearful that the cycle might repeat, but he also hopes that by breaking the chain, he can reclaim a sense of reliability in his own body and regain the ability to be present with his students, his family, and the community he has devoted his life to.
